answers.answer:
Short answer: SCOPe's treatment of Prp8 (chain A of PDB 3jb9, the 3.6 Å cryo-EM structure of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe intron-lariat spliceosome, Yan et al. 2015) splits this ~2,400-residue protein into five structural domains rather than treating it as one unit. Four of the five map onto previously classified SCOP/SCOPe superfamilies that are shared with mobile group II intron proteins and other well-known enzyme families, and one (the large N-terminal region) matched nothing in the existing hierarchy and was curated as a new fold. The decomposition therefore shows Prp8 to be an evolutionary mosaic: a scaffold assembled from the domains of a group II intron-encoded maturase/reverse-transcriptase plus two further nuclease-like/metalloprotease-like modules, all of which have lost catalysis, grafted onto a lineage-specific N-terminal domain with no detectable ancestry outside the spliceosome.

The domains and their classification (SCOPe 2.07 era curation; I am answering from memory, so individual sid/sunid numbers should be checked against the release):

1. N-terminal domain (roughly residues 1–~870): a large, mostly α-helical/mixed region that embraces the 5′-exon/U5 snRNA region of the spliceosome. SCOPe found no structural match to any existing fold and classified it as a newly observed fold with its own new superfamily and family. This is the 'new' component: there is no outside protein from which function or structure can be transferred, and the fold assignment rests on a single moderate-resolution cryo-EM model, so it carries more uncertainty than the X-ray-backed domains.

2. Reverse-transcriptase-like (RT, 'fingers/palm') domain (~residues 880–1300 in yeast numbering): classified with the reverse transcriptases in the multi-domain class, superfamily e.8.1 (DNA/RNA polymerases), as a Prp8-specific family. This is the key homology link to the group II intron-encoded protein (maturase/RT), predicted by Dlakić & Mushegian (2011) and confirmed by the Prp8 crystal structure (Galej et al. 2013). Prp8 lacks the catalytic YADD motif, so it is a degenerate, non-polymerizing RT: the superfamily assignment supports common ancestry and shared architecture, not polymerase activity.

3. Endonuclease-like (En) domain (~residues 1650–1830): a type II restriction endonuclease-like (PD-(D/E)xK) fold, placed in the Restriction endonuclease-like superfamily (c.52.1). This again parallels the group II intron protein, whose C-terminal 'En' domain is a DNA endonuclease of the same fold. The catalytic acidic residues are not conserved in Prp8, so nuclease activity must not be transferred from superfamily membership.

4. RNase H-like domain (~residues 1830–2090): classified in the Ribonuclease H-like superfamily (c.55.3, within the ribonuclease H-like motif fold), consistent with the earlier X-ray structures of this isolated domain (PDB 3e9o/2zkc, Pena et al. 2008; Ritchie et al. 2008). It is related to RNase H, integrases and transposases at the superfamily level but is catalytically inert; its role is RNA binding/positioning of the catalytic core, so only structural (not enzymatic) homology should be inferred.

5. Jab1/MPN domain (~residues 2150–2395, the C-terminal Brr2-binding domain): classified with the JAB1/MPN domain superfamily (c.97.3, cytidine deaminase-like fold), as in the earlier 2og4 crystal structure (Pena et al. 2007). Prp8's MPN domain lacks the JAMM zinc-binding motif of true deubiquitinases, so it is a pseudo-enzyme used as a protein-interaction module; isopeptidase function cannot be transferred from the superfamily.

Evolutionary interpretation: the co-occurrence of RT-like, thumb/linker and En-like domains in the same order as in the group II intron maturase, plus the shared catalytic RNA core chemistry, is the strongest structural evidence that the spliceosomal Prp8 descended from a group II intron-encoded protein. The RNase H-like and MPN domains are additional recruitments from widespread enzyme superfamilies, all retained for RNA/protein binding after loss of catalysis. The N-terminal domain's new fold suggests a eukaryote/spliceosome-specific innovation (or divergence beyond recognition).

Strength of the relationships: the four 'known' domains are related to their respective superfamily members only at the superfamily level (probable common ancestry inferred from structure plus active-site topology), not at the family level, where SCOPe keeps Prp8 domains as separate Prp8 families because sequence similarity to other members is undetectable. Fold-level similarity alone (e.g., any c.55 or c.97 fold member) implies nothing about homology. Practical limits: 3jb9 is a 3.6 Å cryo-EM model, so domain boundaries and the new-fold call are less certain than for the X-ray-derived domains; for template-based modeling, the isolated higher-resolution crystal structures (3e9o for RNase H-like, 2og4 for MPN, 4i43 for the RT/En/RNase H core) are better templates than 3jb9 itself; and function should never be transferred from the superfamily relatives, since every Prp8 enzyme-like domain is a pseudo-enzyme.
